Floor accents are not here either — they come from data/book-colors.json, which holds each book's own colour as stated on mattdinniman.com.

books.title: Dungeon Crawler Carl
books.blurb: Earth is foreclosed on, and the only humans left standing are the ones who happened to be outside. Carl goes down into the dungeon barefoot, carrying a cat.

books.title: Carl's Doomsday Scenario
books.blurb: The Over City is the first floor that behaves like a place rather than a level — and Carl picks up a bomb he can never put down.

books.title: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook
books.blurb: Every subway on Earth, welded into one knot of moving trains — and a manual left behind by the crawlers of an earlier season.

books.title: The Gate of the Feral Gods
books.blurb: Sealed pocket worlds, a portable gate that opens onto things which should not be given doors, and the discovery that the NPCs are people.

books.title: The Butcher's Masquerade
books.blurb: Wealthy aliens buy licences to hunt crawlers for sport. Carl's answer is to hunt them back, on camera.

books.title: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride
books.blurb: A floor that runs on cards, built out of Earth's own dead, where people become playable pieces — and Mordecai's past stops being backstory.

books.title: This Inevitable Ruin
books.blurb: Nine armies, thirty days, one castle, and no respawns. The floor where the dungeon's props declare independence on live galactic television.

books.title: A Parade of Horribles
books.blurb: A racing floor with a worsening track, a system that has started to glitch, and a coming-out party for the ages.

floors.name: The First Floor
floors.premise: Welcome to the first floor! Dirt, corridors, safe rooms, and a tutorial that kills people, which is the most honest kind. Find the stairs before the clock runs out. Kill things. Open boxes. Read the descriptions, or don't. I enjoy it either way.

recap.title: Pink Crocs, a cat, and the end of the world
recap.text: Three in the morning, a Seattle cold snap. Carl cracks a window for a cigarette and his ex-girlfriend's show cat goes out through it and up a tree. He follows her in a leather jacket, boxer shorts and Bea's pink Crocs, and that is the only reason he is standing outside when every building on Earth comes down at once. A voice gives the terms: eighteen floors, each on a clock, and the planet back from the Borant Corporation for whoever reaches the bottom. At the foot of the stairs the achievements arrive in a wall, a Goblin Murder Dozer takes both Crocs, and Carl earns his way into Mordecai's guild hall by landing on a goblin engineer barefoot. Mordecai is an indentured guide, currently a rat, on his seventh or eighth human world, and he has one rule above all: read the description. Then Donut eats the Enhanced Pet Biscuit out of Carl's hand and gets up talking. She has the higher stats, so she takes the party, names it the Royal Court of Princess Donut, makes Carl her Royal Bodyguard, and puts on the Enchanted Crown of the Sepsis Whore while Mordecai is still warning her about it. It enters her in the line of succession of something called the Blood Sultanate, eight floors down. Carl punches a Bad Llama to death in the throat and pockets its meth. He still has no shoes, and the AI, reading out his new Smush skill, is breathing heavily about his feet.

recap.title: Tally, the Hoarder, and the premiere
recap.text: The first safe room belongs to Tally, a Bopca Protector in a paper hat who cooks Carl the best murgh vindaloo of his life and special-orders salmon for Her Royal Highness. The screen over the counter counts crawlers, and it only goes down: ten million, then four. Carl throws goblin dynamite into a Scatterer nest and walks straight into his first boss, the Hoarder: fifteen feet of a woman in torn sweatpants who begs in Spanish and vomits roaches. He strangles her with a dog's leash and punches her until she dies, telling her he is sorry. The loot is spiked kneepads, not pants, and Donut asks whether there is a worst-dressed award. At the edge of the neighbourhood they find Rebecca W, stripped, shot once through a moth tattoo, an apple core in her box and her killer's name on the corpse. Carl decides he wants to find the man who did it. Then the first episode of Dungeon Crawler World airs over Tally's counter: Earth cut down to slums and dumps, forty minutes of people dying, and not one second of the Hoarder. The stairs begin to appear with a warning attached. Go down early and you wait in stasis, forgotten by the audience, until the floor collapses.

recap.title: A meth war and a motorcycle
recap.text: A slime eats Carl's glove and his sleeve, and he has an idea: goblins build vehicles. The Goblin Pass tattoo turns their dots white, and Donut, charisma thirty-seven, reduces the shamanka to tears, sits in her lap and names her Rory. Two bags of llama meth buy the Goblin Copper Chopper, a steam bike with a fur-lined skull for a sidecar, and Donut helpfully tells the goblins where the meth came from. Every goblin in the workshop rolls out to war with the llamas. Carl and Donut strip the empty workshop, push a cart of black powder into the chieftain's chamber and blow it up. There were babies in there. The AI awards You Monster and War Criminal, lets Carl believe for twenty seconds that the babies are fine, and then tells him they are not. You might kill me, Carl decides, but you are not going to break me. Both get the Desperado Pass tattoo, which Donut calls a disqualifying mark. In the next safe room sits Frank Q, whose story is good and wrong in three places. He and his partner Maggie My pull their guns, freeze under the safe-room rules, and the Royal Court rides off leaving a rat corpse behind with lit dynamite in its inventory. A hundred miles east, a sign in red spray paint: stairs + people.

recap.title: Meadow Lark, and a talk show
recap.text: The sign belongs to Meadow Lark, an elder-care home from Wenatchee that came down the stairs whole: the Andrews brothers, Brandon and Chris, who were the maintenance men; Yolanda Martinez, a nursing assistant with a bow; Imani, who has twelve crawler-killer skulls by her name and does not explain them; and Agatha, whom nobody can quite place. Behind them sit more than thirty residents who cannot fight, and the only stairs are guarded by a borough boss rolling around a spiral maze. Carl decides that if he is going to die, it may as well be for something. He and Donut grind, kill the Juicer (Donut opens his neck and breaks her own leg doing it), and come back with a war gauntlet that finally stops Carl breaking his knuckles. The fighters build a redoubt out of goblin tables and weight benches, Brandon calls it the Speedbump, and the Ball of Swine wedges itself on the roof until they stab it apart. Tusklings in tuxedos rain down. Carl kicks one until her health bar goes, and he may be crying. They push open the door at the bottom of the stairs and fall, not onto the next floor but into a production trailer. Lexis blocks out a segment, and Odette, a talk-show host in a crab suit, plays Carl his own catchphrase until he says it. Donut rolls over for the audience and promises they will kill with style. Off air Odette gives them the truth: loot is not always random, the Princess should stay a cat, and her own motive is money.

steps.text: The clock in the corner of every crawler's eye starts at five days. When it runs out the level is reclaimed and everything still in it is forfeit, so the only way to live is a staircase down before then. Focus on anything and an information box opens over it. Signs lead to tutorial guilds, and until a guild has run you through its tutorial the menus stay shut and the loot boxes stay sealed. Boxes open only in a safe zone, and a guild will not open its door while mobs are standing right outside it.

Five days on the clock, and then the level collapses on whoever is left. The floor is nearly the size of the planet's surface, but it is not all connected. A minimap shows the way: you are green, other crawlers blue, NPCs white, mobs red. Nobody can watch this floor live; the cameras open one floor down, and until then there is only an edited premiere and the episodes after it. Stats move on their own until a race and class are chosen, two floors from here. Dead is dead, with no respawning, and going down a staircase heals you to full. The entrances to floor two will not appear until the introductory episode of Dungeon Crawler World has aired, about thirty hours after the dungeon sealed. Restrooms are everywhere, and they are the one place the cameras cannot follow.

The clock runs on five days and the level collapses at the end of them. The floor is close to the size of the planet's surface but not all connected, and nobody watches it live. Dead is dead, and a staircase down heals you. The staircases to floor two stay hidden until the premiere airs. Safe rooms always show on the map, even under the fog of war; inside one, three screens count down to the collapse and to the premiere, and count the crawlers still alive, while a leaderboard waits for the third level to collapse. Sleeping rooms cost nothing, some safe rooms serve food, and boxes may be opened there. A hallway bathroom turns up about every quarter mile, each behind a different door taken from somewhere on Earth, and behind every one of them is the same tiny room with a silver toilet.

Five days to find a way down, and the stairs stay hidden until the premiere airs. Safe rooms show on the map even in the fog; they hold beds, screens, sometimes food, and they are where boxes are opened. Bosses come in tiers, neighborhood, borough, city, province, country and floor, and on this floor there is nothing above city. A boss's lair locks its door once the fight begins, and most boss fights on a floor this shallow cannot be run from. Every boss drops persistent loot that stays on its corpse for any crawler to pick up, and a neighborhood boss's is a map of its neighborhood. Whoever kills it also gets a Boss Box and a star after their name. Dead is dead.

The premiere has aired and the staircases down to floor two are appearing now; on the map they show even where the fog has not lifted. Once down, nobody comes back up. Go down early and you are held in stasis until the collapse, out of sight of viewers who forget fast. The recommended window is the last six hours, which carries no stasis and a head start on everyone who went before. Bosses come in tiers up to city on this floor, lock their lairs once the fight starts, and leave persistent loot on their corpses for anyone. Safe rooms show on the map, hold beds and screens, and are where boxes open. Hallway bathrooms are personal and cannot be shared, and there is one roll of toilet paper per floor.

The clock is under two days. Staircases to floor two are out there, but every borough and city boss sits on one, and the rest are scattered at random and hard to find. Go down any earlier than the last six hours and you wait in stasis until the collapse. In a safe room there is no violence and no stealing: the first offence freezes you for about a hundred seconds, the second for an hour, and the third strips you of everything and drops you in a mob nest. A boss's lair locks once the fight starts, and a gate that closes on a party cuts them off even from the party chat. Bosses leave persistent loot for anyone, and a kill earns a Boss Box and a star. Dead is dead.

The way in is a glowing hole in the ground and an ornate wrought-iron staircase, wide enough for twenty people abreast, carved with fish or demons. At the bottom, on a marble floor, stands a wooden door thirty feet high, carved as a massive fish demon. Past it runs a tunnel as wide and tall as the door, more like a two-lane road than a hallway, lit by torches, humid and around eighty degrees. Branches lead off it. The side halls are narrower, with fifteen-foot ceilings of brick and green lichen glowing on the walls. A neon sign reading Da Tutorial Guild points down a pitch-black alley; the real guild is a plain wooden door further on, with its name painted the colour of the bricks.

Under the iron staircase and the fish-demon door, the dungeon is a maze. The main thoroughfares are torchlit and as wide as a road; off them run tighter halls with low ceilings and glowing green lichen, curving into dead ends, and the minimap draws itself as you walk. Outside the tutorial guild the walls are scorched black where the goblin dozer blew. Hallway bathrooms turn up every quarter mile or so, and tutorial guilds are scattered between them. Near the first safe room the halls open onto a large, round cavern.

The halls have a pattern. The whole region is a grid of equal, giant squares bordered by the wide arteries, twisting and maze-like inside, and every square holds four neighborhoods, each with its own mobs and its own boss. It is a condensed copy of the city above, more organized: the entrance sits at the western edge, near where the Puget Sound was. The goblin neighborhood is where the stairs came down; directly east of it, in the southeast corner of the square, is the Hoarder's, with its round room heaped with garbage; the llamas hold the neighborhood across the hall, and slimes the one north of the Hoarder's. Deeper in the goblin neighborhood, up a dark alley, the goblins keep a workshop with a giant steam engine, six parked murder dozers and a mountain of coal, and a boss door at the far end. The safe room by the Hoarder is a whole fast-food restaurant, playground and all, its windows looking onto solid wall.

East of the city the arteries run on for a hundred miles with nothing in them, through squares that feel like filler at the edge of a map, and walls stand where Lake Washington was above. Safe rooms and training guilds thin out but never stop. The goblin workshop is a blackened ruin behind a wall of burning coal. Far to the east, a red spray-painted sign reads Stairs + People, and the roads begin to curve: this is the edge of a vast circle. At its centre, on the map, is a Stairwell to Floor Two. Between here and there lies the spiral, a round maze of concentric rings, its outer wall broken by half-raised portcullises that look in on a wide inner hall.

The circle around the stairwell is a borough. At the end of one artery a drawbridge crosses to the spiral's main gate, three times the size of the portcullis windows, which open onto nothing: they are sealed with something like thick clay that glows blue when touched. Past the gate is a round courtyard with three exits. Outside it the Meadow Lark camp spreads across the hallway in blankets and wheelchairs. A mile away is a safe room that is a Waffle House from Alabama, full; further on are a safe room with nothing but a candy machine and a Taco Bell from Peru beside a neighborhood of lizard creatures. Two neighborhoods around the circle are already cleared.

Inside the spiral the walls move. The courtyard's walls sink into the ground once the gate shuts, the floor is scored with concentric grooves for the boss to run in and straight lines where walls rise and fall, and new paths open to herd anyone inside onto the track. With the boss dead, every inner wall drops away and the spiral becomes one wide open field the size of a quadrant, purple-lit, with lasers crossing it like a roller rink and the roof rising to a dome. At the very centre a bright light marks the stairwell, ringed by a red forcefield that holds until the last of the boss is dead.

Goblins: four feet tall, green, smart, in leathery rags, armed with clubs that have pineapples on the end, and riding a Goblin Murder Dozer with a pot-helmeted engineer at the controls. Behind the tutorial guild's door is Mordecai, a bearded rat-like guildmaster in a black vest and sandals, who chats with the goblins in their own language and will not let a crawler in while mobs are at the door.

The goblins hold the neighborhood by the stairs, with their engineers and their dozers. Bad Llamas, horse-sized and lava-spitting, will sell you things if you have something worth trading. Level-two rats are everywhere, and cockroaches the size of a loaf of bread, the Scatterers, nest near the first safe room. Mordecai, a Rat Hooligan of level 50, runs the tutorial guild: a non-combatant who was a crawler himself once, born a skyfowl and a changeling since, who takes a new shape each time his guildhall moves. Every other tutorial guild door leads back to his room. The safe room belongs to Tally, a level-63 Bopca Protector in a paper hat and a blue apron, who can make most food a human crawler wants. A crawler who thinks they are speaking their own language is speaking Syndicate Standard, programmed into their brain.

Some mobs are smart and some are not, and the goblins are smart. In this borough they are king, along with the gnolls, the rat-kin and a few others. Their workshop is run by engineers in helmets made of anything to hand, bomb bards who light their dynamite on spiked helmets, and two shamankas, the leader class, whom Princess Donut names Rory and Lorelai; behind the boss door sits their war chieftain. The mobs know the floor will collapse. For them it is only sleep until the next dungeon opens, and they cannot go down the stairs: halfway down, their bodies dissolve. The Hoarder, the boss of the garbage room, is dead. The rats, the Scatterers, the slimes to the north and the llamas across the hall carry on. Tally answers only questions about safe rooms.

The goblin clan has rolled out to war with the llamas over their meth, and its chieftain died in his own chamber with the clan's babies. In the next neighborhood north live the rot stickers, little black ravioli that run on the walls. Rats are everywhere. Other crawlers are the danger now: the first one met is Frank Q, level eight, with three crawler-killer skulls by his name, and his partner Maggie My has five. They hide themselves from the map and tell a good story. Mordecai is still in every tutorial guild, and Tally is still behind his counter.

Around the spiral the crawlers are the night staff of the Meadow Lark eldercare home in Wenatchee and the residents they would not leave. Brandon An and his quiet brother Chris were the maintenance men; Yolanda Martinez is a nursing assistant with a bow; Imani is level ten with twelve crawler-killer skulls she does not explain; and Agatha, homeless, wanders with a shopping cart and a plastic flamingo. Thirty-odd elderly residents, mostly in wheelchairs and walkers, sit in the hallway; about thirty more have settled into the Waffle House safe room, where a gnome cooks and sings for them. Their guide was Mistress Tiatha. Something has been hunting the ones who went looking for other stairs. The next neighborhood over belongs to troglodytes.

The Meadow Lark staff and their residents hold the camp at the spiral's drawbridge, with Agatha and her cart always one step from trouble, and the rest of their people wait in the Waffle House. In the troglodyte neighborhood the Juicer, a lizard bodybuilder, is dead in his gym. The Taco Bell safe room is kept by Sebastian, a Bopca Protector who has fallen for Princess Donut and brushes her hair. Inside the spiral, the boss was never one creature: it was thirty-odd tusklings, the knights and courtesans of the Orcish Supremacy, rolled into one ball. Popped, they rain down in tuxedos and gowns, dazed, short-legged and unarmed.

Traps, starting with the first sign. The neon Da Tutorial Guild points down a black alley where a Goblin Murder Dozer waits: a steam-powered tractor on treads with a spiked, spinning wheel, built to mow crawlers down, carrying goblins with clubs. The dark, narrow hall that looks like the obvious escape probably is not. And the clock, from the moment the doors shut.

Goblin machines: a dozer with a breached boiler counts down and blows, and a shaman's enchantment aims the blast at the nearest non-goblin. Bad Llamas spit balls of lava. Packs of rats bite and poison, and Scatterers swarm in the side halls. Goblins hold grudges and fetch the clan. Fatigue does not heal on its own, and the clock keeps running.

Boss lairs. Damage a boss and its door reforms and bars itself behind you until one side is dead. The Hoarder's garbage room held a fifteen-foot woman who vomits Scatterers, with brood guardians at level four. Goblin dynamite is so volatile a loud noise might set it off. Bad Llamas spit lava, rats poison, and the clock is under four days.

Other crawlers. Frank Q and Maggie My hide from the minimap, wait in a safe room and try to shoot you in it; only the safe room's own rules stop the bullets. Outside, rot stickers run along the walls and ceilings, cling, and explode within three seconds with a blow like a sledgehammer that knocks you down. Slimes dissolve gloves, sleeves and skin, and a punch sinks in to the elbow. Three miles east, a block is overrun with thorny, creeping plants that eat people whole. A goblin clan that has lost its chieftain is coming back. The clock is under three days.

Something has picked off every crawler who left the Meadow Lark camp to hunt for other stairs. The troglodytes in the next neighborhood are fast and venomous, and their poison nearly killed Brandon. Somewhere behind the spiral's wall something pink, fleshy and as wide as the hallway rolls past fast enough to shake the stone, and nobody knows what it is; its gate swallowed a party of police and firefighters, and when it opened again five minutes on, they were gone. Arrows bounce off its sealed windows. And the clock reads forty hours.

The Ball of Swine, a level-15 borough boss: thirty-odd tusklings fused by battle magic into one sphere of pink flesh, eyes and tusks that fills the tunnel floor to ceiling, never loses speed, and rolls over whatever is on its track. The spiral's walls shift to herd you onto that track, and the deeper you go the sooner it comes round. Pop it and what spills out is only dazed tusklings. And the clock, six and a half hours from collapse when the gate shuts.

floors.name: The Second Floor
floors.premise: Floor two! More ground, meaner mobs, spawn limits, and a janitor class of monster that eats whatever you leave lying around and grows. Clean up after yourselves. Or don't. They appreciate it.

recap.title: Moonshine, a Krakaren, and a pair of boxers
recap.text: The second floor opens in a French storm shelter with no Bopca and no food, only a suburban mailbox that answers to Donut: she has joined the Dungeon Book of the Floor Club, and her first book is Second Chance, which raises the dead to fight for her. Carl sees a zombie dog army; Donut sees the best spell ever. The floor above collapses behind them with seven hundred thousand people still on it, and a new rule arrives between episodes: relieve yourself outside a bathroom and a rage elemental comes for your whole party. In a quadrant of moonshining clurichauns Carl adds goblin oil to toilet-grade moonshine, corks it with a torch, and the dungeon names the result Carl's Jug O' Boom. Donut talks two fairy managers out of their filling room and Carl burns the forty workers she leaves behind. Then the Krakaren comes out of a door marked Live, Laugh, Love: a tentacled still whose arms are lined with screaming mouths. They drink a blended fairy to survive her, get drunk, and Donut tells Carl she loves him, not as much as Miss Beatrice or Ferdinand, but she does. A zombie carries in the bomb, Carl wraps himself around the cat under a table, and she drags him out by his cloak. The prize is a pair of boxers with little red hearts that cast Protective Shell. Mordecai is a seven-foot Bugaboo now, and a Borant admin in a diving suit gets told that they will not fight on her schedule.

recap.title: The people train and the Bomb Chicken
recap.text: Meadow Lark has built a train: ten cars of wheelchairs on one glowing chain, pulled by Chris and Imani in pig harnesses. A hundred feet from a safe room, Jack stands up and pees on the wall. Yolanda puts an arrow through his temple a fraction too late, and the level-93 rage elemental that rises out of the stain unravels her and Randall both. Gravity flips. Carl carries Mrs McGibbons along the ceiling under his first Protective Shell, dives through the safe-room door, and goes back out to throw a jug of boom at the thing, which then hammers at the door for hours. Nothing on this floor can kill it, and the rules change so that nobody can sit out the collapse in a safe room. Five hours of work produce the Mother of All Bombs (Brandon calls it the Bomb Chicken), a launcher on a trailer behind the Chopper that drops wheeled bombs Carl calls babies. Imani opens the door, the elemental comes, and with the whole galaxy watching, one man and his ex-girlfriend's cat drag it across an oil slick into the stairwell, where mobs dissolve. Donut Puddle Jumps them clear at the lip. There is no experience, because they did not kill it. They broke the game, and the next announcement patches it.

recap.title: Pork Boy, a dinosaur, and the way down
recap.text: Thirty-six residents go down the stairs in shopping-cart buckets, and Imani, last of all, gives the ceiling her middle finger. Then a substitute admin overrides Zev and puts the Royal Court on Death Watch Extreme Dungeon Mayhem, where an orc talk-show host called the Maestro makes two crawlers, Li Jun and Zhang, gamble on who lives. Carl works out that he is too expensive to punish, walks the whole group off the show alive (Li Jun, Zhang, their boss and Li Jun's sister Li Na), and calls the host Pork Boy on air. The Maestro takes his revenge with footage: Carl's rat-corpse dynamite went off in Frank and Maggie's party, and Maggie My finished off her own daughter, Yvette. On camera he hands Maggie a Legendary potion of Find Crawler, and she smiles for the first time. He also promises to meet them on the ninth floor, as War Leader of the Skull Clan, where the Blood Sultanate is always first out; Donut admits she heard Mordecai tell Carl to leave her there. In the kobold fighting pits Carl feeds a pet biscuit to every caged dingo, the dingoes turn on their masters, and Ralph the Frenzied Gerbil ends under Carl's bare foot. In the reward room Donut chooses seven inches of furious pink feathers: Mongo, a Mongoliensis, who bites her nose until a hornet grabs him and she takes its head off. He is her Royal Steed now. On Odette's couch they learn what a Mongoliensis is. Carl's people called them velociraptors.

floors.previously: On the first floor: Carl survived the tutorial in boxer shorts, which is more than millions of you managed. The cat ate a biscuit, started talking, and took charge. They blew up a goblin workshop, babies and all, bought a motorcycle with llama meth, and adopted an old folks' home: Meadow Lark, stuck behind a borough boss until Carl built them a fort called the Speedbump. Then a talk show on a boat, where Donut made the galaxy scream and a crab called Odette told them loot is not always random. Welcome to floor two.

steps.text: The second floor is laid out like the first: quadrants of rooms and corridors strung along the main hallways, with a boss somewhere in each neighborhood. This time crawlers arrive in the middle of a quadrant, not at the end of a hall. The walls are cinderblock and magically protected, so a punch cracks a block and goes no further. The stairwell down is already marked on the map, deep in the fog. The janitors here are Brindle Grubs, and they eat whatever dead are left lying in the halls.

The floor is laid out like the first, quadrants and neighborhoods strung along the main hallways, with cinderblock walls that crack and never break and the stairwell marked on the map from the start. The clock is six days, the shortest the rules allow, because fewer crawlers came down than projected, and the advice is still to wait until the last moment to descend. Viewers can follow and favorite now. And there is a new law: a human-born crawler who relieves themselves anywhere outside a bathroom summons a Rage Elemental, plucked from the 13th floor, and it kills them and everyone in their party.

Six days to find the stairs, on a floor of quadrants and neighborhoods laid out like the first. Kill a neighborhood boss and its map is yours. Safe rooms are what they say: the AI negates attacks inside them, mobs that wander in are teleported out, and the cameras follow you everywhere except the restroom. Nobody can draw a weapon in front of an admin. Behind the walls the floor is run in 'City' areas, three of them, each with a location manager; one is called Damien. And outside a bathroom, a crawler who relieves themselves still summons a Rage Elemental for the whole party.

Six days, quadrants and neighborhoods, a map from every neighborhood boss, safe rooms the mobs are teleported out of. The janitors have a rule of their own. Every corpse can spawn anywhere from one to fifteen new grubs when no janitor is nearby, and that includes the grubs' own corpses. Destroying a body only stops the grubs from growing on it. There is a cap of 5,000 to a quadrant, and once it is reached the swarm stops homing on corpses and hunts crawlers instead. It is there to stop anyone camping in one place: keep moving. The bathroom law still stands.

Six days, quadrants and neighborhoods, a map from every neighborhood boss. Corpses spawn grubs, up to 5,000 to a quadrant, and the dungeon calls that design rather than a bug. The bathroom penalty holds for the rest of the floor and lifts when it collapses. Safe rooms are still safe, and the larger ones have twenty rooms to rent, free on this floor, but no longer for the whole stay: every safe room and safe area now closes one hour before the collapse, and anyone inside is put out into the hall. A second timer on the board counts down to the closure.

The floor is half gone, and the guides may now explain the third floor and how race and class selection works. A neighborhood boss still holds its neighborhood's map, safe rooms still close an hour before the collapse, and the bathroom law holds until the end. Two loopholes are shut. A non-sapient mob that blunders into a stairwell no longer dissolves on the stairs. And while every corpse still spawns new Brindle Grubs, each grub now has only an even chance of reaching the pupa stage.

The second floor looks like the first done over in a different palette: white floors, orange-tinted lichen on the walls, and cinderblock in place of stone. The arrival point is the middle of a quadrant. Curved hallways run off toward bigger rooms, and the stairwell sits far to the northeast, an icon in the fog. Off the main hallway, in the wrong direction from the stairs and past a quadrant of floating Mind Horrors, is a safe room that looks like an old storm shelter. It has restroom signs in French, televisions on the walls, fifty dusty cots, no food, no Bopca, and a suburban mailbox on a pole.

White floors, orange lichen, cinderblock walls. The main hallways are narrower than on the floor above, and inside the quadrants the concrete is cracked and littered with sharp little rocks. The storm-shelter safe room sits off the main hallway. The stairwell's own quadrant has a tutorial guild and a second safe room just beyond the stairs, and it belongs to the clurichauns: rooms lit by torches, and a big filling room where a tube runs along the ceiling from the boss chamber into a filthy aluminium bathtub of moonshine. In one corner stand two child-sized exercise bikes rigged as blenders. The boss's door, separate from the stairwell, looks like the entrance to a community center, with 'Live, Laugh, Love' in cut-out wooden letters over a schedule of events.

White floors, orange lichen, narrow main hallways, and cracked concrete in the quadrants. In the stairwell's quadrant the clurichauns' filling room and the lair behind it are burned out: melted slag, ductwork hanging in tatters, a small moonshine still with copper tubes running to the huge dead Krakaren against the back wall, and a cage that filled half the room, packed with fried grubs. The tutorial guild is a few hundred meters away. The storm-shelter safe room is back off the main hallway, and the stairwell is close by.

White floors, orange lichen, narrow main hallways. In the stairwell's quadrant the clurichaun lair is burned out and the tutorial guild sits a few hundred meters off. Along a hallway at the edge of the quadrant, bordering the kobolds' quadrant, is a second kind of safe room: Big Shot Chicken, a dusty fried-chicken restaurant with booths, a counter and a Bopca Protector behind it, and sleeping rooms through the back. The storm shelter is three-quarters of a mile away. Grubs fill the halls in their thousands, drifting in from the south.

The stairwell is a large, round chamber with a very high ceiling. The stairs themselves are a hole in the ground as wide as one of the tunnels, with no railing, and a bright light shines straight up out of it. Grub pupae ring the walls. The hallways leading to it are scorched black from end to end where the moonshine burned, and just around the corner at the far end is the tutorial guild. A quarter mile off is Big Shot Chicken, the restaurant safe room on the border of the kobolds' quadrant, and further off is the burned-out lair of the clurichauns.

The stairwell is a large, round chamber with a very high ceiling and a lit hole in the floor where the stairs go down, its approach scorched black, the tutorial guild around the corner. Big Shot Chicken sits a quarter mile off on the border of the kobolds' quadrant. Deep in that quadrant, along its back side, is a safe room that was once an industrial kitchen, with a working walk-in freezer and a toaster that hands out one slice of mana toast per crawler. The kobolds' boss chamber is an old municipal dog pound, its signs in Portuguese: three long hallways lined with cages, then a pair of barn doors into a small fighting arena with a red-stained dirt floor, wooden chairs around it and a pile of bones as tall as the ceiling. Along its back wall is a row of ten cages, a pet reward room.

Brindle Grubs are everywhere: fuzzy, legless worms the size of a cat, black and brown, slow and squeaking. They are the floor's janitors and they eat the dead. In the next neighborhood over, Danger Dingoes patrol the halls. They are the size of mastiffs, with heavy-metal corpse paint on their faces and absurdly long fangs, and where there are dingoes their kobold riders and slave masters are said to be close behind. One quadrant over, Mind Horrors drift through the air like jellyfish: floating brains with tentacles tangled beneath them.

Brindle Grubs everywhere, Danger Dingoes in one neighborhood, Mind Horrors in another. The stairwell's quadrant belongs to the clurichauns: troll-like little hillbilly cousins of the leprechauns, unvaccinated, with oversized heads, patched green overalls, buckled pilgrim shoes, slingshots in their laps and noses that never stop running. They are consultants in Rev-Up, a moonshine business that swears it is not a pyramid. Above them are laminak fairies, managers on hummingbird wings who look like tiny middle-aged soccer moms. At the top is the Krakaren, and the moonshine she sells is in demand in the drinking establishments of the floors below.

Brindle Grubs everywhere, Danger Dingoes and their kobolds in one neighborhood, Mind Horrors in another. The clurichauns and their laminak managers run Rev-Up moonshine for the Krakaren, a shrieking tentacled collective. The one in this quadrant is dead, but she was only a clone: for every one killed, Krakaren Prime births two more. The laminak would like nothing more than to move down to the third floor. The guildmaster of the tutorial guild is Mordecai, a Bugaboo now: a seven-foot, neckless, owl-eyed bear on skinny legs. Bugaboos turn up on the first and second floors, lurking for passing crawlers.

Brindle Grubs in their thousands, Mind Horrors in one quadrant, the clurichauns and laminak of Rev-Up in the stairwell's, under the Krakaren. The quadrant beside the stairs belongs to the kobolds: chihuahuas, near enough, standing upright in chainmail made of beer-can tabs and little spiked caps, carrying feathered spears like lances. They are fearless, and they ride the Danger Dingoes into battle. Mordecai the Bugaboo keeps the tutorial guild.

Brindle Grubs in their thousands, and in their pupae something bigger: hornets as big as people, with grasping clawed hands, that spit acid. These are the Brindled Vespas. Elsewhere on the floor, troglodyte bashers, lizards armed with spiked clubs, hunt in packs. Mind Horrors keep one quadrant, the clurichauns and laminak of Rev-Up the stairwell's, under the Krakaren. The kobolds and their Danger Dingoes hold the quadrant beside it. Mordecai the Bugaboo keeps the tutorial guild.

The kobolds keep their Danger Dingoes in cages and fight them in a pit, and the dingoes come out of it scarred, half-blind and pitiful. Their champion was a frenzied gerbil called Ralph. Now the kobolds of the pit are dead, Ralph is dead, and thirteen dingoes freed by a pet biscuit each run loose through the halls, killing grubs. Behind the arena, ten caged animals wait for a crawler to choose one. Elsewhere: Brindle Grubs and the Brindled Vespas that hatch from them, troglodyte bashers, Mind Horrors, the clurichauns and laminak of Rev-Up under the Krakaren, and Mordecai the Bugaboo in the tutorial guild.

The grubs themselves are harmless: a toddler could kill one. What matters is what they become. The more monsters die in an area, the more the grubs eat, and the more they eat the bigger they get. Once they reach the pupa stage, move on, because their older siblings are not easy to kill. So leave as little of the dead behind as you can. The Danger Dingoes are fast and strong, and the Mind Horrors' psionic attack brings on a headache before you can even see them.

The clurichauns are toxic. Touch one and you can catch the Taint, which stops every kind of healing until it wears off, and they carry slingshots. Their moonshine is 180-proof and explosive; a swig has a 5% chance of killing you outright and an even chance of blinding you. The grubs grow on every corpse left lying around, the Danger Dingoes and Mind Horrors keep their neighborhoods, and the clock is six days. A crawler who relieves themselves outside a bathroom summons a Rage Elemental that kills their whole party.

Bosses can leave their rooms. The Krakaren breaks through her walls with fifteen-foot tentacles, some lined with screaming mouths that open on rows of teeth, one that sprays a green mist of the Vigorous Measles. The cure is a Rev-Up Immunity Smoothie, and making one means blending a laminak fairy into moonshine. The clurichauns carry the Taint, which stops all healing. Leave no corpses for the grubs. And never relieve yourself outside a bathroom, or a Rage Elemental comes for the whole party.

The Rage Elemental is loose. It is level 93, fifteen feet of seething black and purple smoke on six legs with obsidian claws the size of rakes, under a horned badger's skull. Arrows shatter on it, it heals itself, and it can reverse gravity in a stretch of hallway. It is said to dissipate only after claiming 666 souls, and it has already torn through Yolanda and Randall. Around it the grubs have hit their cap: five thousand in a quadrant, swarming crawlers, with bigger level-three grubs among them. Bosses leave their rooms, and the clurichauns carry the Taint.

The grubs are pupating. Their sacs are wet, pulsing mounds as tall as a person, lit red and yellow from inside, each with a timer, and they stand in the halls and ring the stairwell chamber. What comes out is a hornet the size of a human. Before that the grubs reach the cow-tailed stage, twice the size, whipping at you with pointed tails. The Rage Elemental is gone, dissolved on the stairs, but the bathroom law still stands. Safe rooms close an hour before the collapse and put everyone out into the hall, so nobody sits it out behind a door.

Brindled Vespas fill the halls. Each is a hornet as big as a person, with clawed hands that grab and a spit of acid that sizzles on contact. There were so many that the dungeon halved their number and turned the acid down, slightly. Every corpse still spawns grubs, and half of those still pupate. Somewhere on the floor a city boss, a see-through blob the size of a house in a lair of sewer-like tubes, wiped out all of Le Mouvement but one. Safe rooms close an hour before the collapse, and the bathroom law holds to the end.

floors.name: The Over City
floors.premise: Welcome to the Over City! A ruin stacked on top of a ruin, carved into districts and full of people who believe they live here. First floor that's a place instead of a level. Pick a race, pick a class, and try very hard not to get involved in anybody's storyline. You will get involved in somebody's storyline.

recap.title: Races, classes and a manager in a tuxedo
recap.text: Class selection, on the way in. Donut stays a cat, as she always said she would, and on Odette's advice she takes Former Child Actor, a class that lets her try on a new one at every level. She and Odette also arrange, as an accident that is not one, for Mordecai to become her manager, which means he goes where she goes. He will forgive Donut. Carl, no. Carl takes Primal, the race nobody alive remembers the look of, and a class nobody has taken before, Compensated Anarchist: a trap-making, bomb-making social-media dynamo. The floor above collapses mid-selection, leaving just over seven hundred thousand crawlers and eight days on the clock. The Over City is a ruin built on a ruin, full of printed NPCs whose memories are rewritten every time they respawn, guarded by level-75 swordsmen, and signposted by rocks that grow holographic signs when you look at them. Mordecai is an incubus in a tuxedo now, and on his first night in an Over City pub he learns that an incubus's weakness is alcohol. A lemur throws a knife, a quest called The Show Must Go On arrives with trumpets, and Donut drops an eleven-foot stilt clown so Carl can land on it. Their Earth boxes bring Donut a cat tree and a candle, and Carl a Home Depot cactus and eighteen L'Amour westerns like the ones his father kept. His hands shake and he does not know why.

recap.title: Signet, a bear, and the man who became a vine
recap.text: Scouting Grimaldi's Traveling Circus at dusk, they run into the woman from its posters: Tsarina Signet, half naiad, half elf, an Elite with a charisma past a hundred and tattoos that swim. Carl breaks his own pinky to shake off the spell. She needs a sacrifice's blood to raise her paper army, and when Carl breaks his word to her she puts Donut into a magical sleep called Water Lily and keeps her as the price. Carl earns her back the hard way. He kills Heather the Bear, a clown-ridden circus veteran on roller skates, and his lottery ticket casts custard instead of fireball, which heals the parasites out of her and leaves an old bear asking for it to be over. Signet's army breaks the circus defenders but cannot break the big top. Inside it waits Ringmaster Grimaldi: the dwarf who raised Signet, now a Pestiferous Vine, a level-85 city boss and an Elite at once. No crawler this season has faced a city boss and lived. Carl sits in the bleachers, poisons himself, and bleeds on the roots. Then he makes a deal with the producers of Signet's own show, Vengeance of the Daughter: he will play his part in it on the sixth floor if they let tonight go his way. He reads Wisp Armor, eats a cone of worms from a strongman so the vine can speak in his head, and talks Grimaldi into lifting Signet's banishment. She walks into the tent.

recap.title: Family, a pharmacist, and a woman nobody helped
recap.text: Carl gets back to find Donut still asleep and Mongo standing over her in a ring of dead street urchins, full of spikes. With Mongo curled on his lap and the cat breathing on his neck, Carl counts who he has left in the world, and it is everyone in the room. This is my family. The circus vanishes by morning and a stairwell sits where it stood. A Scroll of Upgrade improves Carl's boxers enormously and adds Freeballing, which permits one layer over the crotch, so trousers are now off the table for good. Donut's charisma is past seventy; they build a playbook of named plays, and the Boomy Boy is a clockwork Mongo with dynamite in each hand. In a pub an old orc called GumGum asks for help and Mordecai tells her to go away. Women are being found in the alleys every morning with the blood drained out of them. The next night GumGum is on the ground with her chest torn open, three flying heads trailing their own organs above her, and in her pocket is a letter in necroscript. Mordecai reads the squiggles: a lich problem. Donut decides they are finishing GumGum's quest because GumGum died for it. Meanwhile the Desperado Club opens to them: Clarabelle on the door, Quint the pharmacist, Pustule and her hob-lobbers, and news that Lucia Mar has already been thrown out. The fan boxes deliver a photograph of Bea on her ex's lap, and a jai-alai scoop that finally makes a weapon out of Carl's arm.

recap.title: Danger Zone
recap.text: Carl throws a corpse on Miss Quill's desk as evidence, waves a pass that keeps the swordsmen off him, and while she is picking her beanbag figures up off the floor he fixes her shelf. It is hollow, and he fills it with dynamite. An ambush of city elves and shambling berserkers ends with Carl blind, jumping into a swimming pool full of dead boss, and waking up on a roof. Then comes Danger Zone, a chat show on a boat with Ripper Wonton hosting, a comedian Donut renames Butler, a Naga pop star called Manasa, Princess D'nadia, and Hekla. When the host asks about unrest in the Skull Empire, Carl tells the story of the frog in the pot: if it used to be okay and it isn't any more, kick them out. Barely two minutes pass before the Empire answers with a pulse from Prince Stalwart's yacht, aimed at Carl and Donut's trailer. Manasa had swapped trailers with them. The Valtay, whose worm was driving her dead body, destroy the yacht in return, with the queen consort and the disgraced Maestro rumoured aboard. Mordecai makes a new rule: nobody outside the dungeon gets mentioned again. Back on the ground, elves at a temple proclaim Donut the Oak Fell, She Who Ends, because of an anklet off a dead crawler; Mongo eats a dwarf boy's arm; the temple burns. Hekla asks them to take Katia Grim, a doppelgänger who is ten levels behind, and they do. They feed the lich's letter to a pair of clockwork Mongos as bait and blow Miss Quill's building from a roof away.

recap.title: The Fools Who Broke the Glass
recap.text: Miss Quill dies with her shelves, and Carl is suddenly magistrate of the town. Inside they find the real Featherfall, long dead and mummified in a dreamcatcher of bone, and a meat locker of hanging women who wake up as krasue. The lottery ticket finally lands on fireball. Burgundy, one of the women, lives long enough to explain: Quill ran the town all along, and across the street is her husband, Remex. Remex is not a lich and not a boss. He is a Soul Leech Capacitor, a dead man pulled back to feed his wife the power of the town's soul crystal for an ancient spell called The Final War, and with Quill dead the spell is coming apart. The quest that drops on every crawler within forty-five square kilometres is short: don't die. Carl could run. Instead he closes a Sheol Glass Reaper Case around the cracking gem and puts it in his inventory, where it becomes Carl's Doomsday Scenario: a bomb big enough to flatten a city, which goes off the moment it comes out. Four shocks tear through the district. Magic is stripped from gear, weapons fire where they hang, a ranger dies when his own arrows go off in his quiver, and Donut's crown crumbles to dust on her head, though the succession stays. Carl runs east in a jacket and nothing else, Katia bursts through a wall, and at the bottom of the stairs she presses the detonator. The explosion saves thousands and earns eighty-three crawlers a Celestial box. Borant burns its one veto of the season to void them, a moment after Quan Ch has opened his. On Odette's couch the leaderboard goes up. It is a list of bounties: Lucia Mar first, Hekla second, Carl sixth, Donut seventh.

floors.previously: On the second floor: Carl invented Carl's Jug O' Boom, Donut learned to raise the dead, and a rage elemental unravelled Yolanda because a man named Jack could not hold it in. Carl dragged it into a stairwell behind a bomb-towing motorcycle and broke my game. I patched it. They walked off an orc's talk show alive, called the host Pork Boy on air, and made an enemy for life. Donut adopted seven inches of furious pink feathers named Mongo. Now: races, classes, and a city built on top of a city.

steps.text: The second floor has collapsed, and the third is open: just over seven hundred thousand crawlers, eight days on the clock. Race and class are chosen first, in the game guide's room, and the guide's door no longer opens onto a hallway. It opens onto a village. On the urban levels a guide may step outside, and this is one of them.

This is the Over City: hundreds of small, scattered villages inside wide swaths of abandoned city, all of it connected, about three hundred thousand square kilometres and most of that ruins. Crawlers arrive wherever their guide is, so the whole world is mixed together. Villages have no names, only a size from tiny to extra-large; kill the mayor and you may name it yourself. Level-75 swordsmen keep the villages, but only while the sun is up. There is no jail, only the death penalty, and a crawler who runs from them into the ruins can never return to that village. Inns are saferooms, and saferooms and restrooms are scattered through the ruins too. Tutorial guilds are only in villages; every medium one has one. Focus on a discoloured rock and a holographic signpost grows out of the ground, pointing to settlements, saferooms, restrooms and stairs. There is day and there is night, and the night is worse.

The Over City is hundreds of nameless villages in about three hundred thousand square kilometres of connected ruins. Villages are kept by level-75 swordsmen by day, with the death penalty and no jail, and a crawler chased into the ruins may never go back. Saferooms are pubs now: the food and the five sleeping rooms cost money, ten gold a night. Locator rocks point the way to settlements, saferooms and stairs. And there is a new tab in the interface, Quests: walk into the right ruin and one arrives with trumpets and a box for a reward.

The Over City is hundreds of nameless villages in a sprawl of connected ruins, kept by level-75 swordsmen by day, with the death penalty for anyone who crosses them. Saferooms are pubs that charge by the night, and restrooms are in any pub, some shops, and all through the ruins. The System has made violence against the citizens pointless: a citizen is now worth no experience at all, and the guards have been given a boost. Quests arrive in their own tab.

The Over City is hundreds of nameless villages in a sprawl of ruins, kept by swordsmen by day, with saferoom pubs, locator rocks, and citizens worth no experience. Killing a neighbourhood boss hands over a map of its neighbourhood. And not every stairwell is on the map: many only show themselves once a quest is done, which is how one comes to be standing in the middle of a park where a circus was.

The Over City is hundreds of nameless villages in a sprawl of ruins, kept by swordsmen by day. Quests can be larger than one party. An event quest lands on every crawler inside its zone, and this one's zone is forty-five square kilometres around the swordsmen's soul crystal: sixty seconds to reach a saferoom, then every saferoom in the zone shuts until it is over. NPCs who stay indoors are safe. The quest is called The Fools Who Broke the Glass, and its whole instruction is: don't die.

Out of the guide's door is a bustling village of medieval shops. The streets are wooden slats with wide gaps between them, and smoke drifts lazily up through the holes. The air smells of sulphur and smoke and is hotter than the floor above. Overhead, on a false ceiling, a blazing red sun is rising.

The village is small, shut in by a waist-high fence with a little gate and two armoured guards. Beyond it the ruins begin: crumbling, moss-covered brick slumping in on itself, and buildings of every shape and size fading into a rolling fog. The story goes that this is the top of six layers of a world built inside a dormant volcano, and the floor spans its crater; underfoot, it is all a stage set. A locator rock outside the gate points along the main road to a medium skyfowl settlement thirty-four kilometres off. The nearest stairs are six kilometres away.

A few streets from the Belly-Rubbed Pug, in a park, stands Grimaldi's Traveling Circus: three massive tents, wagons, cages of shadowy shapes and a dozen smaller tents, all inside a five-foot battlement of rock, wood and bone. At dusk the clowns drape skins over the walls and roll barbed wire into the street, and at night the three big tops glow and spotlights wave at the ceiling. The sky is plainly an illusion, and a mortar fired high enough bounces off the rock of the ceiling. Around the park the ruins run on to the skyfowl settlement, thirty-odd kilometres down the main road.

The circus is gone from its park, tents and all, and in the middle of the park stands a staircase down to the fourth floor. The medium skyfowl settlement is easily four times the size of the small village, its buildings much bigger, with eagle folk circling just under the ceiling. Its tutorial guild is a nondescript door a street from a bustling market, and over another street rises a tower with a spinning knife on top: the Desperado Club.

The skyfowl settlement sits behind a wall with gates, thirty kilometres down the road from the small village. Most of its buildings are two storeys or more with big open windows for the fliers, and some stand empty on the ground floor while shops fill the levels above. The Desperado Club takes up a whole street, six storeys of square concrete columns and sunburst reliefs, its neon knife spinning over the top. The magistrate’s building has no first or second floor: it is reached from the rooftops, its third floor is a mall for skyfowl only, and the magistrate’s office sits above that. Directly across the street is a warehouse where the swordsmen go at night. Two blocks away, on a poor residential street, the city elves’ temple is burnt out. West of town the ruins turn to old slums, where the Over City’s version of a YMCA still has its swimming pool, half open to the air.

The magistrate's building and its mall have collapsed into a smoking pile, and the swordsmen's warehouse across the street has a hole through its upper floor. Out of town to the east, past rubble-choked streets, a small, decrepit building holds a stairwell down to the fourth floor. Every crawler within forty-five square kilometres is running for it.

The villages are full of NPCs who think this is the only world there is, because it is. Most were printed by Borant, and their minds are altered every time they regenerate, with false memories planted and inconvenient ones erased. Here they are mostly dwarves, with humans, orcs and elf-like folk among them, all in medieval clothes, and the teenagers swoon at an incubus in a tuxedo. They are said to be the descendants of the few who survived the day a monster at the bottom of the volcano breathed poison, and nine in ten of everyone died or were changed. The ones it changed live in the ruins.

In the villages live the descendants of the survivors; in the ruins, what the cataclysm made of everyone else. Grimaldi's Traveling Circus was the Over City's favourite attraction, and its feral descendants still hold their park: juggling lemurs in painted skulls, giraffes, stilt clowns, short fat clowns and a strongman with a tentacle in his neck. One of the circus's own posters, Tsarina Signet and Her Amazing Battle Squad, has been crossed out and marked Traitor. She is an Elite, half naiad and half high elf, horned and covered in moving tattoos, and her charm took hold of Carl the moment he looked at her.

The circus cannot leave its park, because at its heart is Grimaldi, the man Signet loved, become a vine whose spores ride everything in the circus. Signet lives in a tall white building nearby and attacks the circus every night with a paper army raised by a sacrifice's blood. Tonight the blood was Heather the Bear's, an old circus bear ridden by its parasites for two hundred years. The rest of the night belongs to the ruins' own denizens, red dots all over the map.

The medium settlement belongs to the skyfowl, a little more than half its people: eagle-headed folk about five and a half feet tall, with wings where arms would be and talons for hands, circling just below the ceiling, and their merchants cheat the wingless. Humans, orcs and others live there too. The skyfowl ran the whole Over City before the cataclysm, and their villages keep the old structure without the old oversight. This one answers to Magistrate Featherfall, a dark cleric, whom nobody sees past his assistant, Miss Quill. His building’s mall serves skyfowl and their smaller cousins the chickadees, waited on by harried human and elven women. Every morning dead women turn up in the alleys, strangers to the town, and the city elves of the 201st Security Group, who know crawlers by name before they meet them, are out in the dark looking for them.

The skyfowl hold the settlement, under a dark cleric of a magistrate and Miss Quill at his door. The city elves worship the skyfowl as angels and Apito the Oak Mother as their god, and they recruit from a building marked on the map as a Corrupt Temple, which now lies in cinders. Across the street from it lives a Fathom Dwarf named Eunice with her fifteen or so children, one of them Ricky Joe, short an arm.

Miss Quill was the one running the town, and she is dead. Featherfall had been dead a long time, mummified in a dreamcatcher of bone over a meat locker of hanging women who rose at night as krasue. Across the street, above the swordsmen, sits her husband Remex: a Soul Leech Capacitor, pulled back from the dead to feed her the soul power of the town's crystal for a spell called The Final War, which would have left only the skyfowl and chickadees alive. Now every skyfowl and chickadee in the area is falling ill, most into a coma or worse. Katia is herding the rest of the townsfolk back into their homes.

The guards: level 75, slow, numerous, and the only sentence they hand down is death, so do not attack the NPCs, rob the shops or pass out drunk in the street. The ruins, where the monsters always are and are worse at night. The villages are only safe by day; after dark only the main roads are safe, usually, and the alleys can be worse than the ruins. And the girls with horns, who come out of the woodwork for a high charisma.

The circus’s descendants hunt the ruins around their park. Lemurs throw knives from windows and rooftops and ride giraffes that fling them through the air; the stilt clowns stand eleven feet tall with a butcher knife in each hand and are immune to Fear. The lemurs have already killed crawlers in these streets. At dusk a thousand sentries come home, and the circus’s cauldrons lob purple and yellow mortar rounds that bounce off the ceiling and come down on anything nearby. Tsarina Signet’s charm took hold of Carl at a look, and she needs a sacrifice’s blood. Night comes on quickly here.

Inside the big top waits the circus's master, a level-85 city boss and an Elite at once: a pale-green vine that fills the centre ring to the tent's roof. Its spores and parasitic worms ride every creature in the circus, and a single spore is enough to bring a body back to it. No crawler this season has faced a city boss and lived. Outside, the mortars, the lemurs and the clowns.

Night in the skyfowl settlement: the guards are gone and the alleys are hunting grounds. Street urchins, the ruins’ spiky janitors, come out after dark to clear away corpses and anyone in their way. Krasue, flying women’s heads trailing their own organs, drain their victims of blood; they are ghosts, hurt only by magic, and do not truly die until the body is found. The city elves know crawlers by name, lure pets away with a spell, and lay ambushes in the ruins west of town, with a darkness that swallows torches and snuffs light spells and shambling berserkers, twelve-foot zombies of leftover parts.

The town’s soul crystal is overloading, and there is going to be an explosion big enough to flatten forty-five square kilometres. The saferooms have closed. Under the crystal, hundreds of swordsmen are about to wake at sunrise in a warehouse nobody is meant to be in. Seven minutes.

The bomb is in Carl's inventory, but the spell behind it is still coming apart: four precursor bursts and then a burst of pure wild magic. The first strips the magic from all equipped gear. The second sets every magical weapon off where it hangs, and a ranger dies when his arrows go off in his quiver. The third destroys any armour still worn. The fourth fires the first items in everyone's hotlist on their own. Take off everything magical, and run for the stairs.

A false ceiling · a red sun
